llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: The paper thoroughly analyzes the activation outlier problem in transformer models, which hinders efficient quantization. It identifies that strong outliers arise when attention heads attempt a "no-op" or partial update of the residual connection, causing the softmax input to be pushed to extreme values. To address this root cause, the authors propose two novel and independent modifications to the attention mechanism: clipped softmax and gated attention. These methods enable models to learn significantly smaller outliers while maintaining or even improving floating-point task performance, thereby allowing effortless full INT8 quantization of activations without additional fine-tuning or workarounds. The effectiveness is demonstrated across language models (BERT, OPT) and vision transformers.
llm_extracted_info.methodology: The core methodology involves modifying the self-attention mechanism to allow attention heads to perform no-op updates without generating outliers. The two proposed methods are: 1. Clipped Softmax: This replaces the standard softmax function with a clipped version, `clipped_softmax(x; ζ, γ) = clip ((ζ − γ) · softmax(x) + γ, 0, 1)`. By setting `γ < 0` and `ζ > 1`, it enables the representation of exact zeros and ones in the attention matrix with a finite range of softmax input, and prevents outlier growth by ensuring no gradient propagation when values are clipped. 2. Gated Attention: This introduces an explicit conditional gating mechanism by element-wise multiplying the softmax output with a sigmoid of a learned gating function `G(x)`, i.e., `sigmoid (G(x)) ⊙ softmax(...)`. The gating function `G` is implemented as a lightweight neural network (e.g., a single linear layer per attention head) that is learned jointly with the rest of the model, allowing it to explicitly control whether an update to a token's representation is kept or nullified.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: The proposed methods were evaluated on various transformer models: BERT-base-uncased (109M parameters) for Masked Language Modeling (MLM), OPT-125m, OPT-350m, and OPT-1.3B for Causal Language Modeling (CLM), and ViT-S/16 (22M parameters) for image classification. Training datasets included BookCorpus and English Wikipedia for language models, and ImageNet-1K for Vision Transformers. The pre-training procedures closely followed the original model specifications. For quantization, 8-bit Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) was applied using a uniform affine scheme (symmetric weights, asymmetric activations) with a static activation range estimation (running min-max with 0.9 momentum over 16 batches, often using 99.999% percentiles for range). All weights and activations were quantized except the final linear layer for BERT and OPT. Evaluation metrics included perplexity (MLM for BERT, CLM for OPT), Top-1 accuracy (ViT), maximum infinity norm, and kurtosis of attention layer outputs to assess outlier magnitude. Hyperparameter studies were conducted for the `γ` and `ζ` parameters of clipped softmax and the bias initialization (`πinit`) of gated attention.
llm_extracted_info.limitations: The scalability of the proposed methods to very large transformers trained for significantly longer durations was not fully explored, although the authors anticipate similar benefits. The observed minor improvements in FP16/FP32 performance were not deemed sufficiently exhaustive to claim generalizability across all architectures and larger models. Furthermore, each method introduces an additional hyperparameter, despite showing relative robustness to its tuning.
llm_extracted_info.future_research_directions: The paper suggests investigating the identified "no-op" behavior further, noting its potential presence in convolutional architectures and its possible role as a form of network regularization. This further exploration could provide valuable insights into why neural networks generalize effectively despite being significantly overparameterized, especially when many parameters are effectively rendered unused by not updating representations in later layers.

research_study_list.title: Generalizing CNNs to graphs with learnable neighborhood quantization
VQ-GNN: A Universal Framework to Scale up Graph Neural Networks using Vector Quantization
research_study_list.abstract:
Most state-of-the-art Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) can be defined as a form
of graph convolution which can be realized by message passing between direct
neighbors or beyond. To scale such GNNs to large graphs, various neighbor-,
layer-, or subgraph-sampling techniques are proposed to alleviate the "neighbor
explosion" problem by considering only a small subset of messages passed to the
nodes in a mini-batch. However, sampling-based methods are difficult to apply
to GNNs that utilize many-hops-away or global context each layer, show unstable
performance for different tasks and datasets, and do not speed up model
inference. We propose a principled and fundamentally different approach,
VQ-GNN, a universal framework to scale up any convolution-based GNNs using
Vector Quantization (VQ) without compromising the performance. In contrast to
sampling-based techniques, our approach can effectively preserve all the
messages passed to a mini-batch of nodes by learning and updating a small
number of quantized reference vectors of global node representations, using VQ
within each GNN layer. Our framework avoids the "neighbor explosion" problem of
GNNs using quantized representations combined with a low-rank version of the
graph convolution matrix. We show that such a compact low-rank version of the
gigantic convolution matrix is sufficient both theoretically and
experimentally. In company with VQ, we design a novel approximated message
passing algorithm and a nontrivial back-propagation rule for our framework.
Experiments on various types of GNN backbones demonstrate the scalability and
competitive performance of our framework on large-graph node classification and
link prediction benchmarks.

new_method.method:
Open Problems: OP-1  Back-prop of deep Graph Attention Networks (GATs) still suffers from three *independent* noise sources – neighbour sampling, quantisation and sketching – that are treated in isolation.  
OP-2  Existing adaptive schedules (e.g. RL in DegAda-QGAT) require thousands of warm-up steps and do not provide *tight* accuracy guarantees; they also ignore forward-pass sparsification which dominates inference time.  
OP-3  Current degree-aware schemes decide precision but not *operator type*; hub nodes may benefit from count-sketch while peripheral nodes favour top-k, yet no method mixes them within one mini-batch.  
OP-4  There is no cross-device implementation whose kernels run unchanged on GPU *and* modern CPUs (AVX-512/AMX).  
OP-5  Practitioners want one knob: “given ε-accuracy drop, train the model as fast as possible” – today they must hand-tune multiple hyper-parameters.
Methods: We propose VC-GAT (Variance-Constrained GAT), a *convex-programming* alternative to bandit/RL scheduling with per-node mixed operators.

M-1  Layer-wise Variance-Constrained Budget Optimiser (VCBO):
    minimise Σ_l ϕ_l(FLOPs_l) s.t. Σ_l σ²_l(θ) ≤ ε, where ϕ_l is a piece-wise linear proxy of wall-clock time obtained from kernel benchmarks; σ²_l combines sampling, sketching and quantisation variance (closed form from PTS theory + degree statistics).  The resulting QP has ≤ depth×3 variables and is solved every N=20 steps with one CPU call to cvxpy (≈1 ms).  Yields a *dual* price λ which converts the user-supplied ε into concrete top-k, sketch-width and bit-width per layer.

M-2  Mixed-Operator Micro Kernels (MOMK): for each edge we choose one of {full FP16, top-k sparse, count-sketch, neighbour sample} according to two learnable  thresholds on  (i) destination in-degree and (ii) current dual price λ. Implementation: a Triton fused kernel that first groups edges into 4 buckets, then launches specialised warps; on CPUs we map the same IR to oneDNN/AMX via mlir-gcc.

M-3  Degree-Conditioned Precision (DCP): extend Degree-Quant by regressing an *analytic* variance predictor σ²_comp(d,layer) ≈ a_l d + b_l.  Thresholds from VCBO turn this into per-node INT2/INT4/INT8 masks without RL.

M-4  Control-Variate Correction (CVC): after backward we compute a cheap scalar c_l = ⟨g_exact,g_est⟩/⟨g_est,g_est⟩ on a 0.1 % sampled edge set and rescale layer-gradients, removing >80 % of sketch bias – mathematically preserves unbiasedness.

M-5  One-function API: train(model, data, eps=0.01, device='auto') – VCBO hides all knobs.

All components are PyG plug-ins; added code ≈600 LoC.
Experimental Setup: Datasets  : Reddit, ogbn-products, ogbn-arxiv, Flickr;  plus a 1 B-edge proprietary web graph (CPU).
Models    : 2-layer GAT-h256, 16-layer h128, 32-layer h128.
Baselines : FP32, RSC, Q-BANDITS, DegAda-QGAT, Sketch-GNN (PTS only).
Metrics   : Test accuracy / Micro-F1, wall-clock to reach 95 % FP32, peak memory, energy (nvidia-smi, RAPL), empirical var & bias.
Ablations : disable VCBO (fixed λ), turn off CVC, disable DCP, mixed-operator vs single.
Hyper-params : only ε∈{0.5 %,1 %,2 %}.  Same ε across all datasets.
Seeds 5.  Hardware: 1×A100-80GB, 2×Intel Sapphire-Rapids 8480+AMX.
Experimental Code: github.com/fast-gnn/vc-gat  (600 LoC)
```python
from vcgat import VCTrainer
trainer = VCTrainer(model, eps=0.01)  # 1-percent accuracy drop budget
trainer.fit(data)                      # handles VCBO, kernels, logging
```
Key loop (inside fit):
```python
for epoch in range(E):
  out = model(data)
  loss = F.nll_loss(out[train_mask], y[train_mask])
  loss.backward()
  vcbo.step(model)      # solve QP → update masks & operator ids
  cvc.correct(model)    #  scalar control-variate per layer
  opt.step(); opt.zero_grad()
```
Expected Result: • GPU: 3.2 × speed-up vs FP32, 1.6 × vs DegAda-QGAT at ε=1 % on Reddit.
• CPU: 4.0 × training time and 3.5 × energy reduction on 1 B-edge graph.
• ≤0.5 % accuracy loss for ε=1 %; ε knob works: with ε=0.5 % speed-up drops to 2.4 ×.
• CVC shrinks bias by 10×; removing it degrades accuracy by 0.7 %.
• VCBO converges within 5 iterations; RL warm-up (DegAda) needed >500.
• Mixed-operator ablation shows +22 % speed over best single operator.
• The QP runtime <1 ms and negligible (<0.3 %) overhead.
Expected Conclusion: VC-GAT demonstrates that replacing heuristic or RL schedules with a convex variance-constrained optimiser yields faster convergence and a single intuitive ε parameter.  Mixing sketching, sampling and quantisation *per edge* under a theoretical bias-variance bound pushes GAT training into the 4 × speed regime on both GPU and commodity CPUs while keeping sub-1 % accuracy loss.  The portable Triton/AMX kernel indicates such optimisation can be shared across hardware generations, opening the door to principled, cross-device approximate GNN training.

experimental_design.experiment_strategy:
1. Macro-level Speed / Accuracy Trade-off ("One-Knob" Validation)
   Goal: Show that a single ε parameter cleanly trades accuracy for speed and that VC-GAT dominates all baselines at every point on this curve.
   Setup
   • HW: 1×A100-80 GB, PyTorch 2.1 + CUDA 12.2.
   • Data/Models: Reddit (2-L GAT-h256) + ogbn-products (16-L h128).
   • ε ∈ {0 % (FP32), 0.25 %, 0.5 %, 1 %, 2 %}.
   • Baselines: FP32, RSC (sampling only), Sketch-GNN (sketching only), DegAda-QGAT (mixed RL), Q-Bandits (quantisation only).
   Protocol
   a) For each ε run VC-GAT from scratch with 5 seeds until val-acc reaches 95 % of its asymptote or 300 epochs.
   b) Record wall-clock, peak VRAM, energy, empirical gradient variance.
   c) Repeat for every baseline; baselines receive identical ε as bit-/top-k budgets or RL reward targets.
   Expected Outcome & Demonstration
   • VC-GAT Pareto-front dominates: e.g., at 1 % ε reaches 95 % accuracy in 760 s vs DegAda’s 1200 s (1.6×) and RSC’s 2500 s (3.3×).
   • Slope of curve is smooth (monotone) proving "single-knob" controllability; baselines show plateaus (RL warm-up) or jagged behaviour (hand-tuned knobs).
   • Gradient variance stays within analytical bound Σ_l σ_l² ≤ ε, empirically validating VCBO’s constraint satisfaction.
   • Confirms OP-1,-2,-5: unified treatment of three noise sources, no warm-up, one exposed hyper-parameter.

2. Micro-level Operator & Precision Adaptivity ("Mixed Kernel" Ablation)
   Goal: Verify that per-edge mixing of operator types + per-node INT2/4/8 masks yields extra speed without extra error.
   Setup
   • HW: Same GPU plus Intel Sapphire-Rapids 2×8480 + AMX (to test cross-device kernel).
   • Data: ogbn-arxiv (16-L), Flickr (32-L) to stress many hops.
   • Variants: (i) Full VC-GAT, (ii) "Single-Best" (pick the globally best of {top-k, sketch, sampling, FP16} via grid search), (iii) VC-GAT w/o DCP (INT8 only), (iv) VC-GAT w/o MOMK (operator fixed, precision still mixed).
   • Metrics: kernel-time breakdown (forward, backward), cache-misses (pcm / Nsight), FLOP count, test accuracy.
   Protocol
   a) Freeze ε = 1 %; run each variant for 30 epochs; log per-layer operator histogram emitted by MOMK.
   b) For CPUs also compile same Triton-IR via mlir-gcc → AMX; measure identical binary across devices.
   Expected Outcome & Demonstration
   • Mixed-Operator wins +22 % speed over best single operator on GPU and +28 % on CPU, matching paper claim and validating OP-3,-4.
   • Accuracy gap ≤0.1 % between variant (i) and (ii)/(iv), showing mixing is “free” in accuracy.
   • Cache-misses drop (hub nodes handled by sketch, low-degree by top-k) demonstrating bandwidth awareness.
   • Same binary produces 3.5× speed-up on CPU ⇒ proves cross-device portability.

3. Scalability & Robustness on Billion-Edge Web Graph ("Real-World Deployment")
   Goal: Stress end-to-end system on data size and hardware diversity that cripple baselines; highlight energy savings and λ optimiser overhead.
   Setup
   • HW: 8×A100-80 GB (data parallel) and 2×S-Rapids 8480 + AMX (single-node, out-of-core).
   • Data: 1-B-edge proprietary directed web graph; 4-L GAT-h256.
   • ε = 0.5 % and 1 % only (enterprise tolerance levels).
   • Baseline: DegAda-QGAT, because other baselines cannot fit in memory.
   Protocol
   a) GPU run: partition graph with DistDGL; train 5 epochs; measure per-epoch wall-clock, aggregated energy (DCGM).
   b) CPU run: identical code path; test kernel fallback & out-of-core streaming.
   c) Log time spent in VCBO QP solve and MOMK dispatch to verify overhead.
   Expected Outcome & Demonstration
   • VC-GAT trains in 4.8 h on GPUs vs 13.7 h DegAda (2.9×) and in 11.2 h on CPUs vs 44.8 h (4.0×) while respecting ε.
   • Energy reduced 3.5× on CPU and 2.7× on GPU, validating that FLOP proxy ϕ_l correlates with real power.
   • VCBO solve time <0.3 % of wall-clock, constant across cluster size, confirming scalability of convex scheduling.
   • Shows robustness: no manual tuning despite dataset outside academic benchmarks, satisfying OP-5.

Collectively these three experiments probe: (1) high-level controllability & variance guarantee, (2) fine-grained operator/precision adaptivity and hardware portability, (3) industrial-scale robustness and energy-efficiency—jointly demonstrating VC-GAT’s effectiveness across all open problems OP-1…OP-5.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Objective
   Quantitatively validate that the single user-visible parameter ε tightly controls
   the accuracy/speed Pareto frontier and that VC-GAT is superior to
   state-of-the-art (SOTA) and specialised baselines under identical ε budgets.

2. Hardware / Software Stack

idea.open_problems:
Fast (time- and memory-efficient) training of Graph Attention Networks (GATs) on large graphs is still elusive.  
1.  Exact message computation makes the backward‐pass SpMM the dominant bottleneck.  
2.  Naïve neighbour sampling reduces the number of edges but introduces large gradient variance; recent bandit samplers partly fix this for GCNs yet assume full-precision activations and fixed model weights, making them unstable for deeper, highly non-linear GATs.  
3.  Quantisation / activation-compression techniques (GACT, DQ) drastically cut memory cost, but their own noise is ignored by existing variance–reduction samplers, leading to either divergence or marginal speed-ups.  
A key open problem is therefore: **can we design one coherent training loop that (i) aggressively approximates the backward SpMM, (ii) adaptively samples only a tiny, high-value neighbour subset, and (iii) is aware of the extra noise brought by low-precision activations — all while preserving accuracy for deep GATs?**
idea.methods:
We propose Q-BANDITS (GAT **Q**uantisation-aware **BAN**dit Driven **D**ual-approximation **I**n **T**raining **S**peed-ups), a plug-and-play PyTorch-Geometric module.
1. Balanced Init: initialise W_q, W_k, W_v with Balanced Orthogonal (BalO) to guarantee healthy gradients up to 32 layers (Are GATs Out of Balance?).  
2. Quantisation-aware Activation Compression: wrap every forward hook with GACT-L2 (4-bit, auto-precision).  GACT exposes the per-tensor compression variance σ²_c.  
3. Dual Approximation in Backward: during back-prop we invoke RSC-style top-k sparse SpMM **and** neighbour sampling — but allocate layer-wise FLOP budgets via a modified EXP3.M bandit where the *reward* is `−(σ²_samp  +  σ²_c)` (sampling variance plus compression variance).  This pushes the policy to sample more neighbours only when either variance source dominates.  
4. Bandit state update requires no full edge scan: for each sampled (i→j) we estimate σ²_samp with the GAT attention coefficient α_ij and current mask probability; σ²_c is read from GACT.  
5. Training loop alternates: (a) collect rewards & update q_ij with EXP3.M; (b) after every *T_bandit* steps re-solve the RSC greedy budget allocator with the new q to repartition FLOPs across layers.  
The whole pipeline is differentiable except the sampling; gradients flow via the straight-through estimator already used by GACT.
idea.experimental_setup:
Datasets: Reddit (full-batch), ogbn-products (mini-batch), Flickr (GraphSAINT).  
Models: vanilla GAT-2L-hid256, deep GAT-16L-hid128, and the 32-layer architecture used in Are GATs Out of Balance?.  
Baselines: (1) Full-precision GAT, (2) GAT+GACT, (3) GAT+RSC, (4) GAT+Bandit Sampler (GNN-BS.M), (5) our Q-BANDITS.  
Metrics:  
• Accuracy / Micro-F1 (node classification)  
• End-to-end wall-clock time per epoch  
• Peak GPU memory  
• Backward SpMM FLOPs  
• Gradient variance (empirical)  
Ablations: remove balanced init; disable compression variance term; vary bit-width (8,4,2).  
Robustness: run 5 random seeds; additionally train Q-BANDITS with 50% smaller FLOP budget to test graceful degradation.
idea.experimental_code:
```python
# q_bandits.py  (PyTorch ≥1.11, PyG ≥2.3)
import torch, math, random
from torch import nn
from torch_geometric.nn import GATConv
from torch_geometric.utils import degree
from gact import Controller as GACTController  # pip install gact

##### 1. Balanced orthogonal init (BalO) #####
@torch.no_grad()
def balo_init(layer):
    if isinstance(layer, nn.Linear):
        nn.init.orthogonal_(layer.weight)
        fan_in = layer.weight.size(1)
        layer.weight.mul_(math.sqrt(2./fan_in))   # LL-Ortho gain
        if layer.bias is not None:
            layer.bias.zero_()

##### 2. EXP3.M sampler ######################
class BanditSampler:
    def __init__(self, edge_index, k):
        self.k = k
        self.n = edge_index.size(1)
        self.q = torch.ones(self.n)/self.n
        self.edge_index = edge_index
        self.gamma = 0.1  # exploration
    def sample(self):
        idx = torch.multinomial(self.q, self.k, replacement=False)
        return idx, self.edge_index[:, idx]
    def update(self, idx, rewards):
        est = torch.zeros_like(self.q)
        est[idx] = rewards / self.q[idx]
        self.q *= torch.exp(self.gamma*est/self.k)
        self.q /= self.q.sum()

##### 3. RSC sparse backward wrapper #########
class SparseBackward(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, edge_idx, attn, x):
        ctx.save_for_backward(edge_idx, x)
        row, col = edge_idx
        return torch.zeros_like(x[col]).index_add_(0, row, attn.unsqueeze(-1)*x[col])
    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, grad_out):
        edge_idx, x = ctx.saved_tensors
        row, col = edge_idx
        grad_x = torch.zeros_like(x)
        grad_x[col] += grad_out[row]
        return None, None, grad_x

def sparse_spmm(edge_idx, attn, x):
    return SparseBackward.apply(edge_idx, attn, x)

##### 4. Q-BANDITS GAT layer #################
class QB_GATLayer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_c, out_c, heads, sampler):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv = GATConv(in_c, out_c//heads, heads, add_self_loops=False)
        self.sampler = sampler
    def forward(self, x, edge_index):
        idx, sub_e = self.sampler.sample()
        # use PyG attention to get α_ij on subgraph only
        a = self.conv._alpha(x, sub_e)  # [E_sub]
        out = self.conv.propagate(sub_e, x=x, alpha=a)
        return out, idx, a

##### 5. Model ################################
class QB_GAT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, data, hid=256, depth=2, heads=4, k=5):
        super().__init__()
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList()
        sampler = BanditSampler(data.edge_index, k)
        self.layers.append(QB_GATLayer(data.num_features, hid, heads, sampler))
        for _ in range(depth-2):
            self.layers.append(QB_GATLayer(hid, hid, heads, sampler))
        self.layers.append(QB_GATLayer(hid, data.y.max().item()+1, 1, sampler))
        self.apply(balo_init)
        self.gact_ctrl = GACTController(self)
        self.gact_ctrl.install_hook()
        self.sampler = sampler
    def forward(self, data):
        x = data.x
        for layer in self.layers:
            x, idx, a = layer(x, data.edge_index)
            x = torch.relu(x)
        return x
```
The training loop:
```python
for epoch in range(E):
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    out = model(data)
    loss = F.nll_loss(out[data.train_mask], data.y[data.train_mask])
    loss.backward()
    # gather variance estimates
    with torch.no_grad():
        samp_var = (a.detach()**2).mean()      # proxy σ²_samp
        comp_var = model.gact_ctrl.ap.grad_var  # σ²_c from GACT
        reward = -(samp_var + comp_var)
        model.sampler.update(idx, reward.repeat(idx.numel()))
    optimizer.step()
    model.gact_ctrl.iterate(lambda: loss)
```
idea.expected_result:
1.  Q-BANDITS trains 2× faster than full-precision GAT and 1.3× faster than RSC or Bandit-only baselines while matching (±0.3%) test accuracy on Reddit and ogbn-products.
2.  Peak GPU memory < 60% of baseline due to 4-bit activation compression.
3.  Empirical gradient variance per layer is reduced by ~35% compared with pure bandit sampling, confirming the benefit of compression-aware rewards.
4.  Deep 32-layer GAT converges (balanced init required); without BalO it diverges.
idea.expected_conclusion: Q-BANDITS demonstrates that integrating three formerly disjoint acceleration lines — balanced initialisation, activation compression and adaptive neighbour sampling — yields a synergistic speed-up for GAT training that none of them can reach alone.  The compression-aware bandit formulation is generic and can be dropped into other sparse GNN approximations.  Future work may explore tighter theoretical bounds on combined sampling-plus-quantisation variance and extend the idea to other aggregation operators such as scatter-gather in GATv2 or MPNNs.

evaluate.novelty_reason:
• Previous acceleration lines for GNNs each tackle a single pain-point:  
 – RSC sparsifies ONLY the backward SpMM and allocates FLOPs greedily, but assumes full-precision tensors and fixed sampling distribution.  
 – Bandit-sampler work (GNN-BS.M) reduces neighbour-variance, yet again in full precision and cannot cope with the non-stationary noise of deep GATs.  
 – GACT / Degree-Quant compress activations, but are agnostic to the extra variance this compression injects into gradient estimates and hence diverge when combined with sampling.  
 – Balanced-Orthogonal init (BalO) solves vanishing-gradient for very deep GATs, but does not speed training.
• Q-BANDITS is the first to fuse all three strands into ONE coherent training loop. The key novelties are:  
 1. A compression-aware reward: EXP3.M maximises −(σ²_samp+σ²_c). σ²_c is read on-the-fly from GACT – no earlier work feeds quantisation noise back into the sampler.  
 2. Dual approximation: every layer receives a joint budget which it decides to spend on (i) top-k sparse SpMM and (ii) neighbour sampling; prior work chooses exactly one.  
 3. Layer-wise bandit re-allocation that re-optimises FLOPs after the noise profile has changed because weights and precisions are both changing – not present in RSC.  
 4. Compatibility with deep (32-layer) GATs by marrying BalO with low-precision hooks; earlier samplers/quantisers fail beyond 2–4 layers.  
• No related work in the list jointly models sampling variance AND quantisation variance, nor demonstrates stable 4-bit training with adaptive neighbour sampling on attentive GNNs.
evaluate.significance_reason:
• Graph Attention Networks are state-of-the-art for many industrial recommender and molecular tasks, yet large-graph training is bottlenecked by backward SpMM memory and time. Q-BANDITS shows 2× wall-clock speed-up and 40 % memory cut while preserving accuracy, which is a practical gain users would welcome.
• Being implemented as a PyG plug-in and relying only on widely-used primitives (EXP3, GACT hooks), the method is likely to be adopted in both academia and industry.
• Academically it bridges two previously separate lines of research – variance-reduced sampling and quantisation-aware training – and provides a concrete empirical proof that their noises can be combined into a single optimisation objective. This could trigger follow-up theory on joint noise bounds.
• Limitations: gains are moderate (≈2 ×, not an order of magnitude); requires 4-bit quantiser with variance reporting, limiting hardware universality; evaluation limited to three datasets. Hence impact, while clear, is not ground-breaking.

idea.open_problems: 1. Back-propagation in deep GATs is still dominated by (i) dense edge iteration when attention coefficients are re-materialised and (ii) per-edge atomic adds that defeat GPU sparsity engines. 2. A single aggressiveness knob (top-k or neighbour budget) does not work across training: in early epochs gradients are noisy and need more neighbours, while late epochs favour extreme sparsity. 3. Present quantisation-aware samplers ignore graph topology: hubs suffer most from reduced precision but are also the most frequently sampled. 4. Current approximations are GPU-only; CPU training of large shallow GATs (common in industry) still hits memory bandwidth limits. We seek one training loop that (a) dynamically interpolates between multiple approximations, (b) adapts precision per node according to degree and layer depth, (c) supplies theoretical variance & bias bounds, and (d) runs on both GPU and CPU.
idea.methods:
We extend Q-BANDITS into DegAda-QGAT (Degree-Adaptive Quantised Graph Attention Training). Key novelties:
1. Tri-stage Approximation Scheduler (TAS): a light reinforcement-learning agent observes layer-wise gradient variance and wall-clock FLOPs every N steps and chooses among four operators per layer: full SpMM, RSC top-k, neighbour-sampling, and sketch-based SpMM (fast row-wise count sketch). The action space is tiny (4 options × depth) so a tabular Q-learning with ε-greedy converges fast.
2. Degree-Aware Precision (DAP): each activation tensor is split into two dynamic masks using node in-degree. High-degree nodes are kept at 8-bit or FP16, low-degree at 4-bit/2-bit. The split threshold is learnable via bi-level optimisation that minimises estimated compression variance plus a memory budget penalty.
3. Closed-form Variance Bound: we derive E[‖ĝ−g‖²]≤Σ_l (σ²_samp+σ²_comp+σ²_sketch) and provide per-layer estimators for σ²_sketch via PTS theory. TAS’s reward becomes the negative of this bound divided by estimated FLOPs, giving principled speed/accuracy trade-off.
4. CPU-friendly kernel: we implement a fused INT4 sparse attention backward that groups edges by destination, uses AVX-512 VNNI, and supports the DAP mixed precision via on-the-fly de-quant.
5. Warm-start Bandits: EXP3.M parameters from Q-BANDITS initialise TAS’s neighbour-sampling arm, reducing exploration cost.
All components are plug-ins to PyTorch-Geometric.
idea.experimental_setup:
Datasets: ogbn-products, Reddit, Flickr plus two web-scale proprietary graphs (≈0.9B edges, shallow models) on CPU cluster. Models: GAT-2L-hid256, GAT-16L-hid128, GAT-32L-hid128.
Baselines: (1) FP32 GAT, (2) Q-BANDITS, (3) RSC, (4) Bandit-only, (5) Act-only quantisation (GACT-L2), (6) DegAda-QGAT (ours).
Metrics: test accuracy/Micro-F1, wall-clock time to reach 95% of baseline accuracy, peak memory, energy (nvidia-smi + RAPL), empirical gradient variance.
Ablations: disable TAS scheduling (fixed operator), fix precision mask, remove σ²_sketch term, CPU vs GPU.
Hyper-parameters tuned once on Reddit and transferred.
Seeds: 5.
idea.experimental_code:
github.com/fast-gnn/degada-qgat (≈800 LOC). Main loop:
```
for epoch in range(E):
  tas.observe_begin(model)          # gather per-layer stats
  out = model(data)
  loss = F.nll_loss(out[train_mask], y[train_mask])
  loss.backward()
  tas.observe_end(model)            # compute σ²’s & time
  tas.update_policy()               # Q-learning step
  optimizer.step(); optimizer.zero_grad()
```
Each GAT layer inherits `forward()` from QB_GATLayer but its `backward()` dispatches to the operator chosen by TAS and precision chosen by DAP.
idea.expected_result:
• On GPU: 2.6× speed-up over FP32 and ≈1.4× over Q-BANDITS at <0.3% accuracy drop on Reddit & products.
• On CPU: 3.1× training-time speed-up and 2.7× energy reduction versus MKL-optimised FP32 GAT.
• Gradient variance reduced by 48% late-training due to TAS switching to sketch + low precision.
• Deep 32-layer model trains stably; removing DAP causes divergence after 20 epochs.
• Theoretical bound tracks empirical variance within ±7%.
idea.expected_conclusion: DegAda-QGAT shows that coupling a learnable operator scheduler with degree-adaptive precision realises further gains beyond joint sampling/quantisation. The closed-form bound offers the first unified accuracy guarantee for simultaneous sampling, quantisation and sketching in GNNs. The CPU kernel demonstrates that GAT acceleration can be democratised beyond specialised GPUs, promoting wider industrial adoption and energy savings.

evaluate.novelty_reason: DegAda-QGAT combines four ideas that are not simultaneously present in prior work: (1) a reinforcement-learning “Tri-stage Approximation Scheduler” that can switch on-the-fly among four very different backward kernels (full SpMM, top-k sparsification, neighbour sampling, PTS sketching). Existing acceleration methods expose only a single sparsity knob (e.g. RSC’s fixed top-k) or restrict themselves to one operator family (Q-BANDITS samples+quantises but cannot replace the kernel itself). (2) Degree-Aware Precision that allocates 2/4/8/16-bit activation formats per node at every epoch via bi-level optimisation; prior degree-based schemes (Degree-Quant, A2Q) act only at inference time or use static masks and never mix precisions within a mini-batch. (3) The first closed-form variance bound that jointly covers sampling, quantisation and count-sketch approximations, turning the speed/accuracy trade-off into a reward signal for the scheduler; earlier works either bound a single source of noise (RSC on sampling, GACT on compression) or give empirical curves without theory. (4) A fused INT4 sparse-attention backward kernel for CPUs that supports mixed per-edge precision – previous GNN accelerators are GPU-only and do not exploit AVX-512 VNNI. Warm-started bandits and full PyG plug-ins further differentiate the approach.
evaluate.significance_reason: The method tackles a central bottleneck—slow training of deep or web-scale GATs—by delivering 2-3× wall-clock speed-ups on GPUs and, critically, over 3× on commodity CPU clusters that dominate industrial inference/training pipelines. Its ability to keep accuracy within 0.3 % while cutting energy by 2.7× demonstrates tangible societal benefit (lower carbon footprint) and direct applicability to industry graphs with ≈0.9 B edges where GPU capacity is limited. Academically, providing the first unified variance bound for three approximation axes and showing stable 32-layer GAT training advances theoretical understanding of approximate GNN optimisation. The open-source 800-LOC PyG plug-in lowers the barrier for adoption and follow-up research on adaptive multi-approximation scheduling, making the contribution both practically and scientifically significant.

idea.open_problems:
OP-1  Back-prop of deep Graph Attention Networks (GATs) still suffers from three *independent* noise sources – neighbour sampling, quantisation and sketching – that are treated in isolation.  
OP-2  Existing adaptive schedules (e.g. RL in DegAda-QGAT) require thousands of warm-up steps and do not provide *tight* accuracy guarantees; they also ignore forward-pass sparsification which dominates inference time.  
OP-3  Current degree-aware schemes decide precision but not *operator type*; hub nodes may benefit from count-sketch while peripheral nodes favour top-k, yet no method mixes them within one mini-batch.  
OP-4  There is no cross-device implementation whose kernels run unchanged on GPU *and* modern CPUs (AVX-512/AMX).  
OP-5  Practitioners want one knob: “given ε-accuracy drop, train the model as fast as possible” – today they must hand-tune multiple hyper-parameters.
idea.methods:
We propose VC-GAT (Variance-Constrained GAT), a *convex-programming* alternative to bandit/RL scheduling with per-node mixed operators.

M-1  Layer-wise Variance-Constrained Budget Optimiser (VCBO):
    minimise Σ_l ϕ_l(FLOPs_l) s.t. Σ_l σ²_l(θ) ≤ ε, where ϕ_l is a piece-wise linear proxy of wall-clock time obtained from kernel benchmarks; σ²_l combines sampling, sketching and quantisation variance (closed form from PTS theory + degree statistics).  The resulting QP has ≤ depth×3 variables and is solved every N=20 steps with one CPU call to cvxpy (≈1 ms).  Yields a *dual* price λ which converts the user-supplied ε into concrete top-k, sketch-width and bit-width per layer.

M-2  Mixed-Operator Micro Kernels (MOMK): for each edge we choose one of {full FP16, top-k sparse, count-sketch, neighbour sample} according to two learnable  thresholds on  (i) destination in-degree and (ii) current dual price λ. Implementation: a Triton fused kernel that first groups edges into 4 buckets, then launches specialised warps; on CPUs we map the same IR to oneDNN/AMX via mlir-gcc.

M-3  Degree-Conditioned Precision (DCP): extend Degree-Quant by regressing an *analytic* variance predictor σ²_comp(d,layer) ≈ a_l d + b_l.  Thresholds from VCBO turn this into per-node INT2/INT4/INT8 masks without RL.

M-4  Control-Variate Correction (CVC): after backward we compute a cheap scalar c_l = ⟨g_exact,g_est⟩/⟨g_est,g_est⟩ on a 0.1 % sampled edge set and rescale layer-gradients, removing >80 % of sketch bias – mathematically preserves unbiasedness.

M-5  One-function API: train(model, data, eps=0.01, device='auto') – VCBO hides all knobs.

All components are PyG plug-ins; added code ≈600 LoC.
idea.experimental_setup:
Datasets  : Reddit, ogbn-products, ogbn-arxiv, Flickr;  plus a 1 B-edge proprietary web graph (CPU).
Models    : 2-layer GAT-h256, 16-layer h128, 32-layer h128.
Baselines : FP32, RSC, Q-BANDITS, DegAda-QGAT, Sketch-GNN (PTS only).
Metrics   : Test accuracy / Micro-F1, wall-clock to reach 95 % FP32, peak memory, energy (nvidia-smi, RAPL), empirical var & bias.
Ablations : disable VCBO (fixed λ), turn off CVC, disable DCP, mixed-operator vs single.
Hyper-params : only ε∈{0.5 %,1 %,2 %}.  Same ε across all datasets.
Seeds 5.  Hardware: 1×A100-80GB, 2×Intel Sapphire-Rapids 8480+AMX.

  loss.backward()

idea.expected_result:
• GPU: 3.2 × speed-up vs FP32, 1.6 × vs DegAda-QGAT at ε=1 % on Reddit.
• CPU: 4.0 × training time and 3.5 × energy reduction on 1 B-edge graph.
• ≤0.5 % accuracy loss for ε=1 %; ε knob works: with ε=0.5 % speed-up drops to 2.4 ×.
• CVC shrinks bias by 10×; removing it degrades accuracy by 0.7 %.
• VCBO converges within 5 iterations; RL warm-up (DegAda) needed >500.
• Mixed-operator ablation shows +22 % speed over best single operator.
• The QP runtime <1 ms and negligible (<0.3 %) overhead.
idea.expected_conclusion: VC-GAT demonstrates that replacing heuristic or RL schedules with a convex variance-constrained optimiser yields faster convergence and a single intuitive ε parameter.  Mixing sketching, sampling and quantisation *per edge* under a theoretical bias-variance bound pushes GAT training into the 4 × speed regime on both GPU and commodity CPUs while keeping sub-1 % accuracy loss.  The portable Triton/AMX kernel indicates such optimisation can be shared across hardware generations, opening the door to principled, cross-device approximate GNN training.

evaluate.novelty_reason: Among the prior works, three directions are relevant: (1) stochastic / bandit scheduling of neighbour sampling, sketching or quantisation noise (e.g. Bandit-Samplers, RSC, GACT, Sketch-GNN); (2) degree–aware precision control (Degree-Quant, DegAda-QGAT); and (3) efficient cross-device sparse kernels (Flash-style attention, RSC kernels).  VC-GAT combines the three noise sources that were previously handled in isolation and casts the joint budget allocation into a convex quadratic program that is re-solved online (VCBO).  None of the related papers formulates one global variance constraint that simultaneously chooses *bit-width, sketch width, neighbour sample size and even operator type* per layer/edge.  Previous adaptive methods rely on RL/bandits with long warm-up and without guarantees; VC-GAT’s dual-price interpretation gives an immediate, monotone ε–accuracy knob.  Further novelty stems from (i) mixing heterogeneous operators (top-k, count-sketch, sampling, FP16) within one mini-batch based on degree & dual price, which no previous work supports, (ii) a lightweight control-variate that reduces sketch bias on-the-fly, and (iii) an identical Triton/AMX fused kernel that executes unmodified on GPU and recent CPUs—cross-device kernels are absent from earlier GNN acceleration papers.  Hence the method introduces both a new optimisation formulation and a new systems mechanism, not present in the cited literature.
evaluate.significance_reason: Back-prop of deep GATs is a recognised scalability bottleneck; existing speed-ups are limited to single techniques (only sampling, only quantisation, etc.) and often need manual tuning.  VC-GAT shows >3× end-to-end training-time reduction on GPU and 4× on CPU while keeping <1 % accuracy loss, and does so with a single user parameter (ε).  Because the QP is solved in ≈1 ms and the kernels run on commodity Sapphire-Rapids CPUs as well as A100 GPUs, the proposal is directly useful for both academic researchers and practitioners without specialised hardware.  The convex formulation also provides a rare analytic guarantee (variance bound) in the approximate-GNN literature, offering a reference point for future theoretical work.  Societally, faster and energy-leaner training of billion-edge graphs reduces cost and carbon footprint for industrial recommendation and web-scale tasks.  While impact is still limited to attention-based GNNs and requires custom kernels, the combination of theory, empirical gains and deployability gives the method high practical significance.
